title: Talarico conspiracy theory is the latest to blow up in MAGA’s face | CNN Politics
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE:Stream the CNN & Jubilee Town Hall with James Talarico live Wednesday, October 14 at 8p ET with anAll Access subscription.

Source: CNN

Two weeks ago, GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri saw his conspiracy theory about former special counsel Jack Smithimplode spectacularlyat a congressional hearing for all to see.

Rather than seemingly learning a lesson from that episode, the MAGA movement in recent days embraced another sketchy theory that quickly fell apart — that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was missing from the campaign trail because of a mental health episode.

There have been plenty of such episodes this year. And it’s hardly just random social media accounts.

The Talarico example is especially astounding for its reach. The idea that Talarico’s lengthy absence from the campaign trail was not due to the flu (as his campaign said), but rather a mental health episode quickly spread far and wide.

Over just a few days, it went froman admitted rumor; to some like former Los Angeles GOP mayoral candidate Spencer Prattclaiming theyhad actual sources; to winks and nods fromTalarico’s GOP opponent Ken PaxtonandPresident Donald Trump; to right-wing sitescoveringthestill-baselessclaims; to some attempted independent journalism that has been repeatedlypromotedby ElonMusk.

By Sunday afternoon, a pair of right-wing influencersshared audioof what they said was a call with a mental health center in Ohio seemingly confirming that Talarico had just been released from its facility.

“Looks like he was just discharged this evening,” a voice is heard saying. “That’s why I don’t have it.”

The story then exploded on the right. But it just as quickly fell apart:

Some on the right are nowdeleting theirposts aboutthe false claim. Others like former Trump adviser Caroline Wren arewalking back the significanceof the claim.

One of the two right-wing influencers who shared the audio, Nick Sortor,appeared at the White House last yearduring a roundtable on antifa.

For what it’s worth, asCNN’s Andrew Kaczynski has noted, Talarico did a virtual event on September 30 where he said he had the flu and looked physically unwell. He was then off the campaign trail for nine days — not the two weeks that many on the right have claimed — before reemerging publicly on October 9. Talarico also has type 1 diabetes, whichcan make flu symptoms worse.

But for the MAGA movement, this is merely the latest conspiratorial episode.

Two weeks ago, it was Schmitt presenting what he seemed to view as smoking-gun evidence that Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024 and — the theory seemed to go — might have been coordinating with local prosecutors who had indicted Trump in Fulton County, Georgia.

Except it turned out Smith was actuallyat a basketball game in Marylandthat night. And even if he was in Atlanta, it would haveproven basically nothing.

Back in July, MAGA figures led the charge inembracing rumorsand evenflat-out claimingthat GOP Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky — an unpopular figure among Trump supporters since he declared the president lost the 2020 election — was brain dead, amid his much-longer absence from public view. GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin even cited a claim thata photo of McConnell was AI-generated, before later backing off. A GOP House member even said hedidn’t know whether McConnell was alive.

McConnell later returned to the Senate.

Over the summer, many on the right embraced Trump’s baseless conspiracy theory that vandals had sabotaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. A conservative reporterposted supposed video proof. Trump’s Justice Department even indicted a former Olympian. But the Justice Department later acknowledged that the damage “was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism.”

In June, Republicans far and wide — including elected officials — suddenly promoted theories suggestingvoter fraud was to blame for Prattfailing to make the runoff in the Los Angeles mayor’s race.

Except the theory rested on acomplete misreading of the dataand was debunked even by Trump’s DOJ and a top local GOP official. Pratt’s showing was also very much in line with how Republicans usually perform there. And, strategically, it would havemade no sensefor incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to rig the system to promote a fellow Democrat, who would have a better chance at beating her in the runoff than Pratt.

And in February, many on the right shared supposedly damning evidence from right-wing influencer Nick Shirley citing 30 allegedly illegal voter registrations at a UPS Store in San Diego. Those promoting the story includedDonald Trump Jr., who accused the media of ignoring it.

Butfact-checkers notedthat the UPS Store was actually on the ground floor of a mixed-use building with residential units above it. California elections officials said none of the registrations used the UPS Store’s suite number.

Of course, it’s entirely possible that the people promoting these theories don’t necessarily believe them — and that they just see value in promoting them, regardless of how true they are. Some MAGA influencers, after all, continued to promote Schmitt’s theoryeven after it fell apart.

It would seem especially expedient to promote such rumors about Talarico, given he has continued to lead Paxton in some Texas Senate polls and could give Democrats a crucial win in their quest for a Senate majority.

Or, as one participant on anX Spaces eventabout the Talarico story put it on Sunday: “Whether it’s true or not, people deserve to know the potential of this.”

Regardless of whether these people have a gullibility problem, the MAGA echo chamber now has a well-established credibility problem.

This story has been updated with additional developments.
